## Information for Authors

* Abstract submission deadline: **April 15, 2026**
* Submission as **oral** or **posters**
* Abstracts have to be submitted in English.
* The length of the abstract is limited to **2,000 characters** (including spaces), the length of the **title to 250 characters** (including spaces).
* Use only common abbreviations as referenced in the [Oxford Dictionary of Abbreviations](https://www.oed.com/information/understanding-entries/abbreviations/?tl=true). If you use your own abbreviations, they must be written out in full the first time they are used.
* The abstract should use the following structure as far as possible: **introduction, methods, results, conclusion/outlook**.
* You can upload a maximum of **two additional files** containing either tables or graphics.
* You can add up to **5 keywords** to your post.
* When preparing your contribution, please make sure that the spelling, grammar, gender and diversity-sensitive language is correct. The contributions will be printed as submitted; there is no proofreading. After submission, contributions can be edited until the end of the abstract submission.
* The posters will be presented as printed version on poster boards on site.
* The decision on acceptance/rejection of an abstract and its classification in the program is made by the scientific committee based on the review results.
* The authorship will be informed in June 2026. Organisational details will be communicated directly to the authors.
* To present your paper, you must register for the congress for the fee and pay the registration fee in due time.

```{r}
#| label: extract_results
#| echo: false
#| message: false


library(posterior)
library(HDInterval)
library(brms)
library(metafor)

data = read.csv("../data/study_data_leadIQloss.csv")

freq_mean <- round(as.numeric(freq_model$beta), 2)
freq_lb <- round(as.numeric(freq_model$ci.lb), 2)
freq_ub <- round(as.numeric(freq_model$ci.ub), 2)

# tau2 for frequentist model
freq_confint <- confint(freq_model)
freq_confint <- freq_confint$random

m.brm_samples <- as_draws_df(m.brm)
Bayes_mean <- round(mean(m.brm_samples$b_Intercept), 2)

hdi <- hdi(m.brm_samples$b_Intercept, credMass = 0.95)
Bayes_lb <- round(as.numeric(hdi[1]), 2)
Bayes_ub <- round(as.numeric(hdi[2]), 2)

# calculate tau2 and I2 analogous to metafor
# Extract posterior samples of tau
tau_samples <- as_draws_df(m.brm, variable = "sd_author_year__Intercept")
tau_sq_samples <- tau_samples$sd_author_year__Intercept^2

# Get the SAME typical within-study variance that metafor used
vt <- freq_model$vt

# Calculate I² using metafor's approach for each posterior draw
I2_samples <- tau_sq_samples / (tau_sq_samples + vt)

# Summarize tau²
tau_sq_mean <- mean(tau_sq_samples)
tau_sq_median <- median(tau_sq_samples)
tau_sq_ci <- quantile(tau_sq_samples, c(0.025, 0.975))

# Summarize I²
I2_posterior_mean <- mean(I2_samples)
I2_posterior_median <- median(I2_samples)
I2_credible_interval <- quantile(I2_samples, c(0.025, 0.975))
```

## Abstract
### Quantifying uncertainty: A methodological comparison of Bayesian and frequentist meta-analyses of studies on lead exposure and children's intelligence quotient

**Introduction**: Uncertainty quantification in evidence synthesis is crucial for risk assessment and policy-making, but current meta-analysis approaches often fall short in this regard.
The Bayesian framework provides probabilistic uncertainty quantification.
We compared frequentist and Bayesian meta-analytic frameworks, using lead exposure and IQ as a case study.

**Methods**: We systematically searched PubMed and Scopus for epidemiological studies on blood lead level (BLL) and IQ score in children. 
Risk of bias (RoB) was assessed and regression coefficients were harmonized.
In both meta-analyses, we used random-effects models and included the same effect estimates.
<!-- The frequentist approach used restricted maximum-likelihood estimation. -->
The Bayesian meta-analysis employed a hierarchical model with weakly-informative priors.
Sensitivity analyses examined robustness to RoB and prior specification.
$\tau^2$ and $I^2$ were estimated as measures of between-study heterogeneity.

**Results**: Twelve studies were included after screening.
The frequentist approach yielded a pooled estimate of `r freq_mean` (95% confidence interval: `r freq_lb`; `r freq_ub`) IQ points per unit increase in $\log_e$-transformed BLL (µg/dL).
The Bayesian model yielded a mean pooled estimate of `r Bayes_mean` (95% credible interval: `r Bayes_lb`; `r Bayes_ub`).
Between-study heterogeneity was substantial (frequentist: $\tau^2$ = `r round(freq_confint[1,1], 1)`, $\text{I}^2$ = `r round(freq_confint[3,1], 1)`%; Bayesian: $\tau^2$ = `r round(tau_sq_mean, 2)`, $\text{I}^2$ = `r round(I2_posterior_mean, 3) * 100`%).
The Bayesian framework provided a posterior distribution for heterogeneity, quantifying uncertainty from between-study variation. 
Sensitivity analyses showed robustness to RoB and prior specification.
The Bayesian framework was less sensitive to outlier studies, resulting in a lower pooled effect.

**Conclusion**: We provide updated pooled estimates for the effect of lead exposure on children's IQ.
The Bayesian framework provides posterior distributions, enabling direct probability statements, for example about exceeding risk thresholds, and comparative assessments across pollutants.
These features are of particular value regarding risk assessment and policy-making.
